stories.headline: Fact-Checking at Scale: Building a More Accurate and Efficient Synopsis Factuality System
stories.summary: By Shreya S Ramanujam , Yongce Li , Afshine Amidi , Sina Ghiassian , Benjamin Klein. Introduction Picture this — you’re home after a long day at work and can’t wait to catch up on Bridgerton.
stories.why_it_matters: You log on to Netflix, search for “Bridgerton” and land on this screen: If this sounds familiar, you already know what a synopsis is — it’s a short glimpse into what a viewer can expect to see in a show. This marks a notable development for engineering teams working in big tech.
key_points: Problem & Context: At Netflix’s scale, with thousands of titles, multiple episodes per season and multiple languages, fact-checking all of these by hand simply doesn’t scale.

Technical Implementation: Our current factuality checker feeds a reasoning model everything we know about a title (like metadata and text assets) and asks it to judge synopsis factuality according to a rigorous rubric.

Deployment & Impact: There are two main limitations of this approach that we want to optimize: High cost of long-context reasoning calls: Each decision requires expensive, long-context model calls to reasoning models, which doesn’t scale well when we want to check multiple titles, episodes, languages, and style variants.

stories.headline: NormGym: Evaluating Normative Competence through Social Interaction
stories.summary: arXiv:2611.08613v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Normative competence, the ability to infer socially enforced expectations from interaction and adjust behavior accordingly, is essential for agents operating in unfamiliar human communities. Yet existing evaluations largely test whether agents can recognize or apply norms they may already know, rather than whether they can acquire previously unknown norms from social interaction.
stories.why_it_matters: We introduce NormGym, an interactive benchmark for normative competence in which a newcomer must infer a hidden, arbitrary norm while pursuing its own task in a multi-agent community. This marks a notable development for engineering teams working in technology research.
key_points: Problem & Context: We introduce NormGym, an interactive benchmark for normative competence in which a newcomer must infer a hidden, arbitrary norm while pursuing its own task in a multi-agent community.
Technical Implementation: NormGym contains diverse norms and distinct environments, allowing systematic evaluation of current agents, including large language model (LLM) agents.
Deployment & Impact: We find that normative competence remains challenging: the strongest evaluated LLM achieves a joint task-and-compliance success rate of 55.3%.
